q.q: Why can systems design not begin until analysis is complete?
o: The designer must understand exactly what the system has to do
The client must first write the design document
Programmers are not available until analysis ends
Testing must be completed before design can start
q.why: Design plans how to meet the requirements, so those requirements must already be known and agreed.

q.q: Which would NOT normally be found in a design document?
o: Screen layouts and navigation
The signed acceptance test results
Validation rules for each field
An initial test plan
q.why: Acceptance testing happens at the very end, so its results cannot be in the design document.

q.q: Why must modules be tested both on their own and when joined together?
o: Integration testing is always cheaper than unit testing
Joining modules together always removes any remaining errors
Modules that work alone can fail when they pass data to each other
Unit testing is only ever carried out by the client's staff
q.why: Faults often appear at the interfaces between modules, which unit testing cannot reveal.

q.q: In one sentence, what does the design stage decide?
o: What the new system must do for its users
How the new system will meet the agreed requirements
Whether the new system is worth building at all
Whether the built system matches the specification
q.why: Analysis decides what; design decides how; feasibility decides whether; testing checks.

q.q: What happens to a user requirement that is never designed for?
o: Testers will add it during system testing
It will simply not be built
Programmers will add it during coding
It is automatically met by the data dictionary
q.why: Every requirement should be met somewhere in the design; otherwise it is not built.

q.q: Which group uses the design document as the reference to test against?
o: Testers
Regulators checking legal compliance
Customers using the live system
Senior managers deciding on funding
q.why: The design document is the programmers' blueprint, the testers' reference and the maintainers' record.

q.q: Which answer would score for 'State one item in a design document'?
o: Everything about the new system
How the whole system works for users
The validation required for each input field
A description of the program
q.why: Specific items score; vague answers such as 'how the system works' score nothing.

q.q: Why does a thorough design lower the cost of later maintenance?
o: It removes the need to test the finished system
Problems are solved on paper rather than in code
It allows programmers to skip the data dictionary
It means modules never need to be joined
q.why: A thorough design reduces errors and shortens development.

q.q: Which of these is NOT normally shown on a storyboard?
o: The navigation between screens
The inputs and outputs on each screen
The contents of each screen
How fast each screen loads
q.why: A storyboard is a set of sketches; it cannot convey speed or responsiveness.

q.q: What is the main purpose of walking users through a storyboard?
o: To carry out acceptance testing with real data
To obtain early feedback on the interface and navigation
To train them to use the finished system
To produce the data dictionary for programmers
q.why: The storyboard gets feedback before code is written.

q.q: Which is a genuine disadvantage of storyboarding?
o: Users cannot interact with it as they would with real software
It is expensive and slow to produce for each screen
It requires programming skills to understand it
It can only be produced after development is complete
q.why: Storyboards are static sketches, lacking the interactivity of a prototype.

q.q: In a storyboard, what does each frame represent?
o: One test in the initial test plan
One table in the proposed data model
One module of code in the proposed system
One screen or page of the proposed system
q.why: Each frame represents one screen, with contents, inputs/outputs and navigation.

q.q: How is navigation shown on a storyboard?
o: Decision diamonds with yes and no branches
Numbered processes linked to data stores
A list of field names with their data types
Arrows showing which button or link leads to which screen
q.why: Arrows show routes between screens, including routes back.

q.q: Why does changing a design after a storyboard walk-through cost almost nothing?
o: Nothing has been built yet
The changes are made by testers
Storyboards are produced by software
The client pays for every change
q.why: Because no code exists, changes are cheap.

q.q: What usually follows a storyboard once the navigation has been agreed?
o: A feasibility study
A prototype
Beta testing
Acceptance testing
q.why: Because a storyboard cannot be clicked through, a prototype usually follows.

q.q: A pupil lists 'quick to make' and 'does not take long' as two advantages of storyboarding. How many marks are likely?
o: None, because neither is an advantage
Two, because storyboards are quick and cheap
Two, because they are worded differently
One, because both make the same point
q.why: The same idea given twice earns one mark.

q.q: In a prototype, what is a stub?
o: A test plan entry that has not yet been run by testers
A validation rule that rejects bad data entered by users
A menu option or routine that appears but has no working code yet
A printed report produced at the end of each session
q.why: Stubs are placeholders that let users see the structure before every feature is built.

q.q: How can prototyping help design the data model?
o: By training users on the finished system before go-live
By testing the network speed between the client and server
By focusing on inputs, outputs and processing to reveal the tables needed
By letting users choose between different colour schemes
q.why: Working out the data a prototype must take in and produce shows which entities and links are required.

q.q: Which is a disadvantage of prototyping?
o: A working model reduces misunderstandings with the client
Problems, refinements and enhancements are found earlier
Users are involved and feel ownership of the system
Users can be swayed by appearance and overlook accuracy and security
q.why: The other three options are advantages.

q.q: What is a prototype?
o: A set of sketches of each screen with navigation arrows
An early, deliberately incomplete working model of the system
A central description of every data item in the system
The finished system given to external users before release
q.why: A prototype gives look and feel; storyboards are sketches; beta is pre-release.

q.q: Why might a prototype only work with perfectly correct input?
o: It is written in pseudocode only
Its data dictionary is incomplete
It has been fully acceptance tested
It usually has little or no validation
q.why: Prototypes usually have little or no validation.

q.q: A prototype receipt for a music-tuition service shows the pupil, the tutor, each lesson and the fee. Which tables does this reveal?
o: Pupil and Tutor, with Tutor linking to each fee
Receipt only, holding all of the data together
Pupil, Tutor and Lesson, with Lesson linking the other two
Lesson and Fee, with Fee linking pupils to tutors
q.why: The data on the receipt reveals separate Pupil, Tutor and Lesson tables, with Lesson as the link.

q.q: In a prototype menu, the user types 2 for 'View my bookings' and sees 'Coming soon'. What does this show?
o: The prototype has a validation error
Option 2 is a stub that has not been built yet
Option 2 is an evolutionary feature
Option 2 has failed its unit test
q.why: Only option 1 is built; the else branch is a stub.

q.q: What is the difference between a throw-away and an evolutionary prototype?
o: A throw-away one is refined into the final system; an evolutionary one is discarded after feedback
A throw-away one is tested by users; an evolutionary one is tested only by programmers
A throw-away one is discarded after feedback; an evolutionary one is refined into the final system
A throw-away one is built on paper; an evolutionary one is built using program code
q.why: This distinction is given in the notes as beyond the textbook.

q.q: Why might developers resist making major changes to a prototype?
o: Users never give feedback
Prototypes contain no code
Prototyping can be expensive
Stubs cannot be replaced
q.why: The cost of prototyping may make developers reluctant to change it significantly.

q.q: Users try an early prototype and then expect the finished system very soon. This is an example of…
o: a benefit of using stubs
a disadvantage of storyboarding
an advantage of prototyping
a disadvantage of prototyping
q.why: Users may expect the finished system to be ready soon because the prototype looks real.

q.q: Replacing a free-text 'County' box with a drop-down list mainly applies which HCI principle?
o: Low memory load
Consistency
Error prevention
Feedback
q.why: Restricting choices stops misspellings and invalid entries.

q.q: Which output best suits a principal who needs to spot trends in attendance?
o: A 40-page list of every absence by individual pupil
A detailed list of absences for each form class
A summary chart of weekly attendance by year group
The raw attendance data file exported from the system
q.why: Outputs should match the audience; a manager needs a summary, not detail.

q.q: Why should an interface not rely on colour alone to show an error?
o: Some users cannot distinguish colours, so the meaning would be lost
Colour slows down data entry for expert users
Colour uses too much memory on older computers
Colours are not allowed on data entry forms
q.why: Accessibility: colour-blind users need a text or icon cue as well.

q.q: What is human–computer interaction (HCI)?
o: The study of how people use computer systems
The testing of modules once they are joined
The design of tables, keys and relationships
The process of converting data to a new system
q.why: HCI studies how people use systems and guides usable interface design.

q.q: Why does good input design aim to reduce typing?
o: Typed data cannot be validated
Typing uses more storage than clicking
Every keystroke is a chance for an error
Keyboards are not allowed in forms
q.why: Lists, pickers, defaults and auto-complete restrict entry and reduce errors.

q.q: Keeping the same button positions, colours and wording on every screen applies which HCI principle?
o: Feedback
Error prevention
Low memory load
Consistency
q.why: Consistency means skills learned on one screen transfer to others.

q.q: An error message says 'Postcode must start with BT – please re-enter'. Which HCI principle does this apply?
o: Accessibility
Feedback
Consistency
Low memory load
q.why: Feedback messages say what is wrong and how to fix it.

q.q: Showing menu options on screen rather than expecting users to remember codes applies which principle?
o: Consistency
Error prevention
Suit the user
Low memory load
q.why: Users should not have to remember codes.

q.q: Which answer would earn full credit in a design question?
o: A drop-down list is a good feature to include on any input screen
A drop-down list makes the form look more modern and attractive
A drop-down list of class names should be used on the form for input
A drop-down list of class names prevents spelling errors, so records match
q.why: Name the feature and explain how it helps the user.

q.q: Which three things does output design decide?
o: Content, format and medium of screens, reports and documents
What data is captured, how and on which screen
Who tests, where, and with what test data
Data type, length and validation of each field
q.why: Output design covers content, format and medium matched to the audience.

q.q: Which of these is NOT normally recorded in a data dictionary?
o: The name of the person who typed in each record
The data type of each field
Whether a field is a primary key
The validation rule for each field
q.why: A data dictionary describes the data items, not who entered individual records.

q.q: How does a data dictionary help prevent integration errors?
o: All programmers use the same names, types and formats
It encrypts the data passed between modules
It removes the need for integration testing
It speeds up the network between modules
q.why: Agreed formats mean one module's output matches the next module's expected input.

q.q: Which is the best data type for a field recording whether a member has paid?
o: Date
Real
Boolean
String
q.why: Only two values are possible, so Boolean fits.

q.q: A data dictionary records MemberID with format LL9999. Which value matches this format?
o: EN417
q.why: LL9999 means two letters followed by four digits.

q.q: Which validation rule is precise enough for a data dictionary?
o: Range check: whole number from 1 to 8 inclusive
Range check
Must be a sensible number
Check the number is in range
q.why: 'Range check' alone is not a rule; the limits must be stated.

q.q: Which data type best suits a membership 'Fee' field such as 32.00?
o: Boolean
Integer
String
Currency
q.why: Fee is stored as currency to 2 decimal places.

q.q: A 'Category' field may only hold J, A or S. Which validation check does the data dictionary specify?
o: Length
Presence
Range
Lookup
q.why: Checking a value is in a list of allowed values is a lookup check.

q.q: How does a data dictionary help testers?
o: It lists the actual outcome of every test
They take boundary values straight from the validation rules
It shows which tests passed and failed
It replaces the need for a test plan
q.why: Precise validation rules give precise test data.

q.q: Without a data dictionary, what problem might arise between two modules?
o: The modules could not be unit tested by programmers
One module might store a date as text and another as a date value
Neither module would be able to accept any date input
Both modules would be forced to use the same date format
q.why: Inconsistent formats cause modules to pass data incorrectly.

q.q: A user types their email address twice and the system compares the two. This is…
o: a format check
a consistency check
a lookup check
verification
q.why: Double entry checks the data was keyed accurately – verification.

q.q: Which check ensures a hire end date is after the start date?
o: Presence check
Length check
Range check
Consistency check
q.why: It compares two fields with each other.

q.q: A shop assistant enters a price of £4.59 instead of £5.49. Why might validation not detect this?
o: Both values are reasonable and within the allowed range
The value entered has too many characters
Validation is never applied to prices in a shop
Validation only checks text fields, not numbers
q.why: Validation checks data is sensible, not that it is correct.

q.q: Which check would detect a single mistyped digit in a product barcode?
o: Length check
Range check
Presence check
Check digit
q.why: The check digit is recalculated from the other digits and will not match.

q.q: What is the difference between validation and verification?
o: Validation checks data was entered accurately; verification checks it is sensible and obeys rules
Validation guarantees data is correct; verification only checks that it is present
Validation checks data is sensible and obeys rules; verification checks it was entered accurately
Validation is done by people proof-reading; verification is done automatically by software
q.why: Validation = sensible/allowed; verification = matches what was intended or the source.

q.q: What is a limitation of verification?
o: It always rejects values outside a range
It only works with numeric data
It cannot catch an error copied consistently from a wrong source
It cannot catch any error made while typing
q.why: If the source is wrong, double entry will match the wrong value.

q.q: A PIN must be exactly 4 characters. Which validation check is this?
o: Type check
Format check
Range check
Length check
q.why: The number of characters is checked by a length check.

q.q: A car registration must be 3 letters, a space and up to 4 digits. Which check is this?
o: Length check
Type check
Lookup check
Format check
q.why: Matching a pattern is a format check.

q.q: Top-up amounts must be from £1.00 to £50.00. Which check is this?
o: Range check
Lookup check
Type check
Length check
q.why: A value between limits is a range check.

q.q: In a top-up program, the user types 'ten' and sees 'Please enter a number'. Which check has rejected the input?
o: Type check
Format check
Range check
Presence check
q.why: decimal.TryParse fails on non-numeric input, so the type check rejects it.

q.q: When are validation rules decided and where are they recorded?
o: During implementation, in the user guide
During analysis, in the feasibility report
During testing, in the test plan
During design, in the data dictionary
q.why: Recording them in the data dictionary lets programmers code them consistently and testers test them.

q.q: Why is it usually cheaper to fix an error found during unit testing than one found after go-live?
o: Clients pay the full cost of all errors found during unit testing
Errors found after go-live cannot be fixed by the developers at all
The fault is close to where it was made and no live data or users are affected
Unit testing is carried out on cheaper computers than the live system
q.why: Late errors need investigation, patches, re-testing and possibly data repair.

q.q: Two modules each pass their own tests but give wrong results together. Which stage should reveal this?
o: Beta testing
Integration testing
Unit testing
Acceptance testing
q.why: Faults at the interfaces between units appear when they are integrated.

q.q: Which statement about testing is true?
o: Thorough testing proves that software has no errors
Testing can show errors exist but cannot prove there are none
Only the client is allowed to test the software
Testing only happens after development is complete
q.why: No finite set of tests can cover every possible input and path.

q.q: Which is the correct order of testing stages?
o: Unit, system, integration, alpha/beta, acceptance
Unit, integration, system, alpha/beta, acceptance
Integration, unit, system, acceptance, alpha/beta
System, unit, integration, acceptance, alpha/beta
q.why: Testing builds up from single modules to the client's sign-off.

q.q: Which question does acceptance testing answer?
o: Does the complete system meet its specification?
Does it meet the client's requirements with real data, ready for sign-off?
Do tested modules pass data correctly together?
Does each module work correctly on its own?
q.why: These are the unit, integration and system testing questions respectively.

q.q: How do thorough unit tests help when a fault appears later?
o: Later faults cannot occur if unit tests pass
The client no longer needs to do acceptance testing
The search can concentrate on the joins rather than every unit
Integration testing can be skipped altogether
q.why: Confidence in each unit narrows the search to the interfaces.

q.q: When does testing start during development?
o: As soon as the first unit is written
Only once the whole system is built
Only after the client signs it off
Only once implementation begins
q.why: Testing is ongoing, from the first unit to client sign-off.

q.q: Why can integration testing not replace system or acceptance testing?
o: It cannot judge whether the business requirements are met
It tests each module completely on its own
It cannot detect faults at module interfaces
It is only carried out by the client's staff
q.why: Each stage catches faults the previous one cannot.

q.q: A tester enters values and compares outputs with the specification, without seeing the code. This is…
o: acceptance testing
black-box testing
white-box testing
integration testing
q.why: No access to code, inputs v expected outputs – black box.

q.q: What is the main aim of white-box testing?
o: To compare the outputs of the old and new systems
To make sure every path and branch through the code is exercised
To test the software with real users in their setting
To check the user interface is attractive to users
q.why: Knowing the structure lets the tester design tests for each path.

q.q: Integration testing finds an error in one unit. What should happen next?
o: Only the acceptance tests are repeated by the client
The system is released and the fault is fixed later
The unit is removed and the system tested without it
The unit is modified, unit tested again and then re-integrated
q.why: The fixed unit must pass its own tests before being joined again.

q.q: What is the real difference between black-box and white-box testing?
o: Whether the client or the developer pays
Whether the screen or the database is tested
Whether the tester uses knowledge of the code
Whether the tests are run on a computer
q.why: Black-box is not 'without a computer', and white-box does not 'test the screen'.

q.q: Which techniques are typical of white-box testing?
o: Normal, boundary and erroneous data only
Questionnaires sent to external beta users
Dry runs, trace tables and a test per branch
Live data at realistic volumes in the workplace
q.why: White-box testing uses the code's structure.

q.q: A car-park Charge module returns 0 for blue badge holders, hours × £1.20 for up to 2 hours, and otherwise £2.40 + (hours – 2) × £2.00. What is Charge(3, false)?
q.why: 3 hours is over 2, so £2.40 + 1 × £2.00 = £4.40. £3.60 wrongly uses 3 × £1.20.

q.q: Using the same Charge module, what is Charge(5, false)?
For white-box testing of the Charge module, what is the minimum number of tests to exercise every branch?
o: Two
Four
Three
One
q.why: There are three branches: blue badge, up to 2 hours, over 2 hours.

q.q: Where do faults typically occur during integration testing?
o: Inside a single module, in a branch that no unit test exercised
At the interfaces, when one unit sends data in a form the next does not expect
In the data dictionary, when field names are spelt correctly
In the user interface, when screens use inconsistent colours
q.why: Examples include different date formats, units or values passed on that should have been rejected.

q.q: Who usually carries out unit testing?
o: The project manager
External beta testers
The programmer, in-house
The client's end users
q.why: Unit testing is done in-house, usually by the programmer, as soon as the unit is written.

q.q: Which testing is carried out by potential users, without developers present, on a pre-release version?
o: Alpha testing
System testing
Beta testing
Unit testing
q.why: External, realistic environment, pre-release – beta.

q.q: What normally marks the end of acceptance testing?
o: The code is rewritten from scratch
The client signs off the software
The developer starts alpha testing
Beta testers are recruited
q.why: Sign-off formally completes the contract.

q.q: System testing checks the complete system against…
o: the client's live data volumes
the agreed system specification
the beta testers' opinions
competitors' similar products
q.why: System testing is the developer's check against the specification.

q.q: Which is TRUE of alpha testing?
o: It is carried out by members of the public
It never follows a test plan
It takes place in-house at the developer
It happens after acceptance testing
q.why: Alpha is the developer's final in-house phase.

q.q: Who carries out acceptance testing, and where?
o: The programmer, on each module as soon as it is written
Selected external users, on their own equipment at home
The client's end users, in their live working environment
The developer's test team, in-house at the developer
q.why: Acceptance testing is by the client's users with real data in a live setting.

q.q: Why is beta testing especially valuable for software sold to many customers?
o: The developer cannot test every combination of devices
It is carried out in-house by the developer
It replaces the need for system testing
It is always done with the client's live data
q.why: Beta testers use many different devices in realistic settings.

q.q: System testing is essentially which kind of testing applied to the whole product?
o: White-box testing
Black-box testing
Unit testing
Beta testing
q.why: Testers do not need to know how it was built.

q.q: What kind of data is used in acceptance testing?
o: Simulated data created by programmers
Only boundary values from the data dictionary
Test data from the developer's test plan
Genuine data at realistic volumes
q.why: Acceptance testing uses real data volumes.

q.q: A pupil writes that system testing is done by the client against their requirements. What is wrong?
o: That describes acceptance testing; system testing is by the developer against the specification
That describes unit testing; system testing is by programmers on one module at a time
That describes beta testing; system testing is by external users on their own equipment
Nothing is wrong; system testing and acceptance testing are the same thing
q.why: Mixing up system and acceptance testing is the most common slip.

q.q: Which column of a test plan is completed by the tester rather than the test designer?
o: Actual outcome
Expected outcome
What is being tested
Test data
q.why: Actual outcome and pass/fail are filled in when the test is run.

q.q: When should a test be recorded as FAIL?
o: Whenever an error message appears on screen
When the test took too long to design and run
Whenever the test data used is erroneous data
When the actual outcome differs from the expected outcome
q.why: An error message may be exactly what was expected; FAIL means actual ≠ expected.

q.q: What is the main purpose of a test plan?
o: To make testing systematic, covering every requirement, path and validation routine
To train users in how to operate the system before it goes live
To replace the data dictionary with a list of every field and its type
To choose the changeover method that will be used at implementation
q.why: A plan stops testing being random and ensures vulnerable areas are checked.

q.q: Which four components does the mark scheme look for in a test plan?
o: Who tests, where, with what data, against what
Test number, actual outcome, pass/fail, tester's name
Field name, data type, format, validation rule
Part of system tested, what is tested, test data, expected outcome
q.why: These are the four main components; actual outcome and pass/fail are added by the tester.

q.q: After a fault is fixed, why should all the tests be run again, not just the failed one?
o: The failed test cannot be re-run
Tests must always be run in pairs
A fix can break something else
The expected outcomes will have changed
q.why: Re-running all tests (regression testing) catches new faults caused by the fix.

q.q: Tickets cost £8.50 and the largest valid quantity is 8. What expected outcome should the test plan give for quantity 8?
o: Accepted; total £59.50 shown
Accepted; total £76.50 shown
Rejected; quantity too large
Accepted; total £68.00 shown
q.why: 8 × £8.50 = £68.00, and 8 is a valid boundary value.

q.q: How can a systems analyst help with the test plan?
o: By supplying boundary values from the data dictionary and checking results against the specification
By writing the program code for each module and running unit tests on it
By acting as an external beta tester using their own computer equipment
By signing off the system on behalf of the client after acceptance testing
q.why: The analyst supplies test data and checks results against the specification.

q.q: A field accepts whole numbers from 10 to 50. Which pair is boundary data?
o: 10 and 50
9 and 51
0 and 100
11 and 49
q.why: Boundary values are the valid extremes.

q.q: A field accepts whole numbers from 10 to 50. What kind of data is 50.5?
o: Erroneous
Boundary
Extreme valid
Normal
q.why: It is not a whole number and is above the range.

q.q: A price band runs £0–£9.99, then £10–£19.99. Which value tests the edge between the two bands?
q.why: £10.00 is the lowest value of the second band; £9.99 is the top of the first.

q.q: Why is boundary data especially important?
o: Errors such as using < instead of <= appear at the limits
It is the most common data that users will enter
It is always rejected by the validation routine
It tests whether the network can handle the load
q.why: Off-by-one errors only show up at the edges of ranges.

q.q: For a rule 'whole number from 0 to 100', which statement is correct?
o: 0 and 101 are both boundary data
0 is erroneous data and 101 is boundary data
0 and 101 are both erroneous data
0 is boundary data and 101 is erroneous data
q.why: Boundary values must be valid; 101 is outside the range.

q.q: What is the expected result when erroneous data is entered?
o: Accepted with a warning message
Rejected with a helpful message, with no crash
The program stops and restarts
Accepted and processed correctly
q.why: Erroneous data must be rejected gracefully.

q.q: Coursework marks out of 60 are graded U 0–17, E 18–26, C 27–41, A 42–60. Which pair tests the boundary between C and A?
o: 41 and 42
40 and 41
42 and 43
27 and 42
q.why: 41 is the top of C and 42 the bottom of A; every band edge is a boundary.

q.q: Using bands U 0–17, E 18–26, C 27–41, A 42–60, which value is erroneous?
q.why: 61 is above the maximum of 60; 0 and 60 are boundaries and 17 is a band edge.

q.q: For the rule 'senior: 65 or older' with a sensible upper limit of 120, which value is normal data?
o: sixty
q.why: 65 is a boundary, 72 is normal, and 121 or 'sixty' is erroneous.

q.q: Testers try the value just outside a limit, such as 51 for a range of 10 to 50. How should it be recorded?
o: As boundary data that must be accepted
As erroneous data that must be rejected
As extreme data that must be accepted
As normal data that must be accepted
q.why: Values just outside a limit are invalid, so they are erroneous.
